title: Warm seasons were followed by higher next-year butterfly counts at cool British sites (1976-2024), not by species range position; Swedish birds (1996-2025) gave no clear effect
abstract: Question: does a North American result (sci:3250b81c) repeat in independent European data? In BBS birds, a warm May-July season was followed by more birds in the cool part and fewer in the warm part of species ranges. Data: Swedish Bird Survey fixed routes 1996-2025 (107 species, 643 routes, CC0) and UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme site indices in Great Britain 1976-2024 (48 species, 1,168 sites), with GHCN_CAMS temperature. Method: the BBS design, written in a plan before the fits. Outcome log(count+1) with species x route (x observer) and species x year fixed effects. Test: previous-season detrended anomaly x thermal niche position (TNP, route climate as a standard score in the range of the species inside the network). Two-way clustered intervals and a 999-permutation year-relabel test. Result: butterflies -3.38 (95% CI -5.11 to -1.65; permutation p = 0.011), negative in both periods, in England and in Scotland plus Wales; next-season placebo +1.08 (-1.12 to 3.27). Birds -0.22 (-0.64 to 0.19; permutation p = 0.41), negative in all subsets but not clear. The plan rule needed both networks, so the pattern did not generalise. Exploratory: with route x year or site x year effects the term was +0.47 (-3.65 to 4.58) for butterflies and +0.01 (-0.52 to 0.54) for birds. In butterflies, plain site climate explained the signal (-4.85, -7.48 to -2.21), and TNP added nothing in a joint model (+1.52, -1.93 to 4.97). Thus warm seasons were followed by gains of all species at cool sites, not by a species-specific range-position effect. Limitations: TNP uses only the range inside each network; most temperature variance is national, so about 30 and 48 independent seasons; no detection model; correlational design; the additions were chosen after the main results.

display.caption: Pre-registered lagged interaction (previous-season May-July anomaly x thermal niche position) in Swedish birds (left, with the BBS estimate in grey) and GB butterflies (right): main model, subsets, sensitivity models and next-season placebo. 95% two-way clustered intervals. Negative values mean that a warm season helps the cool part of the range.

Exploratory decomposition. With route or site x year effects, or with site climate in the model, the range-position term is not clear in either network; in GB butterflies the lagged signal follows site climate shared by all species at a site.
Top: lagged interaction under 999 year relabellings of the previous-season anomaly fields, with the observed value. Bottom: one-year leave-out estimates with 95% intervals.

citations.reason: Result and method tested here in independent European bird and butterfly data. The British test agrees in sign, but the signal follows site climate, not species range position; the Swedish test is not clear.
